passage.title: 'Dominoes and Decisions', a teacher-written introduction to a philosophical debate for TGA
paras: Imagine a line of dominoes. Push the first, and the last must fall. Some philosophers argue that people are like this: every choice is caused by what came before, so no one could have acted otherwise. If that is true, can anyone be blamed?

Others reply that a person is not a domino. We weigh reasons, feel the pull of conscience and decide. Courts, schools and families all treat people as responsible, because a world without responsibility would be a world without justice.

panels.title: The thought experiment
points: Dominoes make an abstract idea visible
Then the writer breaks it: 'a person is not a domino'
Ends with a practical consequence: justice
Islamic belief: Allah's decree and human choice

keywords.def: the idea that everything is caused and fixed in advance
an imagined situation used to test an idea

questions.q: Summarise each view in one sentence.
questions.a: Determinism: every choice is caused, so no one could act otherwise. Free will: people weigh reasons and are responsible.

questions.q: What practical reason does the writer give for responsibility?
questions.a: Without responsibility, there could be no justice.

questions.q: Core: in the portal response box, write a balanced paragraph: 'Is Macbeth responsible for his crimes?' Use both views. Starter: 'A determinist might argue that... However...'
questions.a: Both views applied to Macbeth (witches and Lady Macbeth as causes; his choices and conscience) and a judgement.

questions.q: Extend: which view does the play support? Use Banquo.
questions.a: Free will: Banquo hears prophecies but does not kill.

questions.q: Stretch: why might a Jacobean audience insist on responsibility?
questions.a: Regicide was a sin and treason; blaming fate would excuse it.

questions.q: Why does the writer use dominoes?
options: To make the idea of fixed causes easy to picture
Because the text is about games
questions.a: A) To make the idea of fixed causes easy to picture. It illustrates determinism; it does not prove free will.

questions.q: Answer the ponder in one sentence.
questions.a: Answers vary; most will argue we can choose, so blame is fair.
